description: We’re a crew of engineers, builders, and problem-solvers who treat Earth’s biggest questions like mission-critical problems. Fueled by curiosity and code, we turn raw NASA data into tools that make a real impact. Every launch starts with an idea, and ours is ready for liftoff. 🚀
summary:
ARES TRAIL delivers a safety-first, suit-tablet EVA (extra-vehicular activity) planner for a two-person Marswalk on the western delta front of Jezero Crater. The application fuses topography, optical imagery, mineral context, a thermal model and a radiation model into a single layered map, then computes a slope- and obstacle-aware route with a complete risk budget. It was built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

This project puts all of that on one screen and turns it into a route.
details:
ARES TRAIL delivers a safety-first, suit-tablet EVA (extra-vehicular activity) planner for a two-person Marswalk on the western delta front of Jezero Crater. The application fuses topography, optical imagery, mineral context, a thermal model and a radiation model into a single layered map, then computes a slope- and obstacle-aware route with a complete risk budget. It was built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

NASA has global and regional Mars maps, but an astronaut on foot needs a hyperlocal picture: where the steep scarps are, which outcrops are worth sampling, how hot the surface will get, how much radiation the walk costs, and how far they are from shelter. This project puts all of that on one screen and turns it into a route.

The default demo scenario is a three-stop EVA from the Octavia E. Butler landing site to Skinner Ridge, Wildcat Ridge and Amalik Outcrop: approximately 6.3 km, 4 h 20 min, 0.11 mSv, with a readiness score of 78 (CAUTION) under default settings. Every number on screen is derived from the loaded terrain grid and the current controls.

The Problem

·       Global and regional Mars maps exist, but an astronaut on foot needs a hyperlocal picture.

·       Key questions: where are the steep scarps, which outcrops are worth sampling, how hot will the surface get, how much radiation does the walk cost, and how far is shelter?

·       The project consolidates all of these onto one screen and turns them into an actionable route.

4. Application Features (Screen-by-Screen)

4.1 Top Bar

The always-visible header is the suit-tablet status strip.

·       Brand - ARES TRAIL, mission short name ARES TRAIL-1 JEZERO.

·       Site readout - mission site and coordinates.

·       Telemetry - SOL, LMST (local mean solar time), habitat surface temperature in deg C/deg F, dust opacity I, season offset, and a red SPE chip when a solar particle event is active.

·       Status pill - readiness GO / CAUTION / NO-GO with the 0-100 score.

·       Actions - open the voice copilot, switch MAP / 3D, toggle the planning and route panels, export the EVA plan as JSON, reset the scenario.

·       On tablets and phones the panel toggles move into the bottom PLAN / ROUTE tabs; the mic stays in the top bar.

·       A small sync dot appears while the terrain is loading.

4.2 Map

The centre of the screen is a Leaflet map using a custom Mars equirectangular CRS so it lines up with NASA Mars Trek tiles.

·       Base layer - HiRISE optical orthomosaic, 25 cm/px, streamed from Mars Trek. If tiles fail, a banner offers a retry.

·       Overlays (toggle and opacity in the left panel): hillshade and elevation, slope hazard, surface temperature, radiation shelter, mineral context, and the Perseverance traverse.

·       Waypoints - pins show a three-letter code (SKN, WLD, AML, HWK, DPT, STH, HAB). Stops in the current itinerary also carry their order number.

·       Route - cyan line with a dark halo, built from the A* path; small dots mark the end of each leg.

·       Readout - hover readout shows latitude/longitude, elevation, slope, local surface temperature in deg C/deg F and current metres-per-pixel.

·       Probe - clicking anywhere drops a marker with a popup containing the coordinates, elevation, slope and surface temperature at that point.

·       Mini layer bar - quick toggles: HILL, SLOPE, TEMP, MIN, RAD, TRV.

·       Controls - zoom (12-17) and a metric scale bar.

4.3 Holographic 3D View

The MAP / 3D switch in the top bar opens a Three.js terrain view built from the same CTX DEM and live layer state. It is lazy-loaded, so the flat map stays the fast default.

·       Terrain - the 304x298 DEM becomes a displaced surface. Vertical exaggeration is adjustable from 1x to 3x (default 1.6x).

·       Layer texture - hillshade, slope, surface temperature, radiation shelter, mineral context and the heritage traverse are composited into the surface texture and update live.

·       Route and stops - the A* route is lifted onto the surface and waypoint beacons show itinerary order.

·       Cameras - ORBIT for a free look, EYE for a 1.8 m astronaut-height view at the selected stop looking toward the next stop.

·       Deep link - ?view=holo (or ?view=3d) opens the 3D view directly; switching views updates the URL without reloading.

4.4 Left Panel - Planning and Configuration

·       Mission brief - objective, site, crew, habitat and rover/cache context.

·       Itinerary - starts and ends at the habitat H; each row shows the stop order, name, straight-line distance from the previous stop and the science stop duration.

·       Optimize order - reorders the stops to minimise risk over the whole loop, reporting orders checked, resulting distance and duration.

·       Data layers - HiRISE is always on; the six overlays each have a switch and an opacity slider.

·       Conditions - local mean solar time (06:00-20:00), dust opacity, season offset, mission sol, solar particle event toggle, buddy-pair toggle and pressurised rover support toggle.

·       Exact reading entry - every slider value is also an editable field (LMST accepts HH:MM, 1430 or decimal hours; dust accepts values such as 0.73).

·       Safety limits - maximum slope, maximum EVA duration, radiation budget and walk-back limit. These feed the routing cost, warnings and readiness score.

·       Data sources - the data provenance list with links, plus the loaded terrain window size, cell size and elevation range.

4.5 Right Panel - Route Readiness

·       Readiness gauge - 0-100 score with GO (80+), CAUTION (60-79) or NO-GO (<60), plus stop count, distance, duration, A* grid size, current LMST/sol and critical/caution counts.

·       Stat grid - total distance, EVA duration (walking + science), radiation dose and percent of budget, walk-back distance vs limit, maximum slope vs crew limit, cumulative ascent, predicted surface temperature range, and the airlock/suit-up allowance.

·       Thermal picture - habitat surface temperature in both deg C and deg F, a plain-language band, a colour scale, and a Jezero-versus-Mars-wide context note.

·       Safety warnings - generated from the current budget: duration, slope, dose, walk-back, low/high temperature, rough terrain, relaxed slope cap, solo EVA and SPE.

·       Traverse legs - collapsible list of each leg with distance, walking time, stop time, maximum slope and dose; exports the full plan as JSON.

·       Waypoint detail - the selected target with a Perseverance image, credit, coordinates, elevation, sol, science rationale, mineral chips, cached sample and actions.

·       Disclaimer - planning aid, not flight use; models vs published data.

4.6 Bottom Dock - Traverse Profile and Timeline

·       Profile tabs - ELEVATION, TEMPERATURE, SLOPE.

·       Profile chart - the value along the whole route against cumulative distance, with grid lines, distance ticks (HAB, km marks) and clickable stop markers.

·       Timeline - proportional bar of prep, walking and science time, with duration labels and a legend.

·       Clock - route distance and duration plus LMST departure to arrival.

4.7 Field Note Modal

·       Large Perseverance image with credit and a coordinate overlay.

·       Facts: elevation, predicted surface temperature, instantaneous GCR dose rate and rover sol.

·       The science rationale and detailed field instructions, plus mineral context chips and the cached sample name.

·       Current conditions (LMST, dust, SPE/GCR state, coordinates).

·       Add/remove from itinerary and close (button, backdrop or Escape).

4.8 Tablet / Phone Layout

Below 980 px, the map stays full screen and the two panels become bottom tabs: PLAN and ROUTE. Selecting a marker opens the route panel automatically. This is the intended 'carried on the surface' form factor.

4.9 Voice Copilot

The mic button in the top bar opens the ARES TRAIL Copilot. It uses the browser Web Speech API for recognition and speech synthesis, so it works in Chrome and Edge with microphone permission. When recognition is unavailable, the same panel accepts typed commands. The copilot is not a separate source of truth: every command calls the same application handlers as the buttons and sliders, and the spoken reply is derived from the resulting state.

ARES TRAIL is a safety-first EVA planner. Every hazard below is paired with a configurable crew limit and a plain-language warning generated from the current route, conditions and terrain. The warnings feed a single readiness score (GO / CAUTION / NO-GO), so the crew receives one decision together with the reasons behind it.

This document lists the dangers the planner guards against, the default crew limits, and how the guardrails are computed.

Dangers Addressed

Danger

How the planner mitigates it

Falls / injury on steep ground

A* routing treats cells above the crew slope limit as impassable and forbids diagonal corner-cutting. Default 18 deg preferred slope, 34 deg hard terrain cap. Warning: Slope above crew limit.

Running out of EVA time (consumables, daylight, contingency)

5 h duration limit covering walking, science and 25 min suit-up prep. Warning: EVA duration over limit, raised to critical if more than 18 percent over.

Radiation overexposure (galactic cosmic rays)

0.2 mSv dose budget with terrain sky-view shielding. Warning: Radiation budget exceeded at over 1x budget (caution) or over 1.2x (critical).

Stranding too far from shelter

4 km walk-back limit, extended by 1.4x when pressurised-rover support is enabled. Warning: Walk-back distance exceeded.

Solar particle event (SPE)

50x dose scenario with a critical Solar particle event warning instructing the crew to shelter at the habitat or pressurised rover.

Cold exposure / hypothermia

Predicted surface temperature below -70 deg C is a caution, below -85 deg C is critical (Cold exposure).

Hot surfaces (suit and hardware)

Surface temperature above 5 deg C on sun-facing slopes is flagged as Warm surface.

Rough terrain / loose scree, twisted ankle

Roughness index above 7 triggers a Rough terrain warning.

No safe route exists

The planner falls back to the 34 deg hard cap and flags the leg (Route exceeds preferred slope) to treat steep sections as no-fall zones.

Solo EVA

Buddy-pair check raises a Solo EVA warning when the second crew member is disabled.

Impossible science targets

Waypoints are snapped to the nearest passable cell, so a stop on a steep outcrop cannot make the whole route impossible.
